⌂
Clinical Reference

Hyperkalemia

On this page
Serum potassium above ~5.5 mmol/L — a silently arrhythmogenic lab value. The heart can arrest with a near-normal ECG, so you treat the rate of rise, the ECG, and the trajectory, not the number alone. The reflex sequence is stabilize the membrane → shift K⁺ into cells → remove K⁺ from the body.
Often asymptomatic Severe ≥ 6.5 mmol/L Peaked T → sine wave → VF / asystole Calcium first · then insulin+glucose · then remove ~98% of body K⁺ is intracellular
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Mechanism — the story

Potassium is the body's most abundant intracellular cation. About 98% of total-body K⁺ sits inside cells (~140 mmol/L intracellular vs ~4 mmol/L in plasma), and that enormous gradient — maintained minute-to-minute by the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase — is the resting membrane potential of every excitable cell. Plasma K⁺ is therefore not a measure of body potassium stores; it is a snapshot of a balance between two systems.

Internal balance (fast, minutes) = how K⁺ is distributed between cells and plasma. Insulin, β2-adrenergic tone, and alkalosis drive K⁺ into cells (by stimulating the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase). The opposite — insulin deficiency, acidosis (H⁺ moves in, K⁺ moves out), cell lysis (rhabdomyolysis, tumor lysis, hemolysis), hypertonicity/hyperglycemia (solvent drag), β-blockade, and digoxin (which poisons the pump) — dumps K⁺ out of cells into the plasma. These shifts move potassium in minutes without changing total body content at all.

External balance (slow, hours–days) = net intake versus excretion. Roughly 90% of K⁺ is excreted by the kidney (the rest by the colon). Renal secretion happens in the distal-nephron principal cells and depends on three things: aldosterone, distal sodium delivery, and tubular flow. Anything that lowers GFR, lowers aldosterone (type-4 RTA / hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism; ACEi/ARB/MRA; heparin), or cuts distal flow impairs excretion — which is why CKD plus a RAAS inhibitor is the archetypal chronic hyperkalemia.

Why the heart is the organ at risk. Raising extracellular K⁺ depolarizes the resting membrane potential toward threshold. Early on this makes cells briefly more excitable — the earliest ECG sign is the tall, tented peaked T wave. But sustained depolarization inactivates fast sodium channels, so the phase-0 upstroke and conduction slow: the P wave flattens, the PR interval lengthens, the QRS widens, and finally the QRS and T merge into a sine wave that degenerates into ventricular fibrillation or asystole. Critically, this can happen with startling speed and a deceptively bland ECG — the ECG is insensitive, and sudden hyperkalemic arrest occurs in patients whose tracing looked almost normal minutes earlier.

Picture plasma potassium as people crowded into a room. You have exactly three moves. (1) Shove people into side-rooms — insulin + glucose, albuterol, bicarbonate push K⁺ into cells. Fast, but they wander back out (rebound) when the drug wears off. (2) Open the exits — loop/thiazide diuretics (renal exit), gut binders (fecal exit), and dialysis (the emergency fire door) actually remove people from the building. (3) Post a bouncer at the cardiac door — IV calcium stands at the heart-muscle membrane and holds it stable, protecting against arrhythmia, but it does not reduce the head-count. In a true emergency you do all three, in order: bouncer first (calcium), then shove into side-rooms (shift), then open the exits (remove).
Potassium homeostasis and the three therapeutic moves. Plasma K⁺ rises from increased load, a shift out of cells, or impaired renal/colonic excretion. Emergency therapy maps one-to-one onto the cascade: stabilize the myocardium (calcium), shift K⁺ into cells (insulin/glucose, albuterol, bicarbonate), then remove it (diuretics, binders, dialysis). Only removal lowers total-body potassium.
The Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase pumps 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in per ATP, keeping ~98% of body K⁺ intracellular. Insulin and β2-agonists stimulate this pump (therapeutic shift); digoxin poisons it (a cause of hyperkalemia in overdose).
BruceBlaus, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0 — source
The nephron. K⁺ is secreted in the distal nephron / collecting-duct principal cells under the control of aldosterone, distal Na⁺ delivery, and tubular flow — the three levers RAAS inhibitors, low flow, and low GFR all disable.
BruceBlaus, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0 — source
Approximate ECG sequence as serum K⁺ climbs. Peaked T waves are earliest; the sine wave is pre-terminal. Because the correlation between K⁺ level and ECG is poor, never withhold treatment on the basis of a normal-looking ECG in a patient with a high potassium.
Real 12-lead ECG in hyperkalemia — narrow-based, tall, tented peaked T waves, the earliest and most recognizable change.
Drs. M-J. Agbayani & E. Gonzales, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0 — source
Pre-terminal sine-wave pattern of severe hyperkalemia — the widened QRS merges with the T wave. This is a peri-arrest rhythm: give IV calcium immediately.
M. Rosengarten, CardioNetworks/ECGpedia, CC BY-SA 3.0 — source
Every therapy in this guide maps to one step above. Calcium = raise threshold potential (membrane stabilization; no K⁺ change). Insulin+glucose / albuterol / bicarbonate = stimulate the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase or correct acidosis to shift K⁺ into cells (temporary). Loop/thiazide diuretics = raise distal Na⁺ delivery and flow to drive kaliuresis. Patiromer / SZC / SPS = bind K⁺ in the gut for fecal loss. Dialysis = direct extracorporeal removal. Keep this map in mind and the whole algorithm becomes deducible rather than memorized.

Classification & causes

📊

Severity bands — societies differ, so both are shown

BandUK Kidney Association 2023Common US / ACLS conventionWhat it means at the bedside
Mild5.5–5.9 mmol/L5.0/5.5–5.9 (up to 6.0)Outpatient work-up; find & remove the cause; recheck
Moderate6.0–6.4 mmol/L6.0–6.4Treat promptly; ECG + telemetry; usually admit
Severe≥ 6.5 mmol/L≥ 6.5, or ≥ 6.0 with ECG changes/symptomsEmergency: calcium → shift → remove; consider ICU/dialysis
Any potassium with ECG changes, symptoms, or a rapid rate of rise is an emergency regardless of the band. A K⁺ of 6.2 that climbed from 4.0 over two hours (crush injury, tumor lysis) is more dangerous than a stable 6.8 in a dialysis patient whose myocardium has adapted. Source: UK Kidney Association 2023.

Acute vs chronic. Acute rises (shifts, AKI, tissue lysis) carry higher arrhythmia risk at any given level because the myocardium has not adapted. Chronic hyperkalemia (CKD, type-4 RTA, RAAS inhibitors) is tolerated at higher absolute levels but is an ongoing outpatient escalation problem.

🧭

Etiology — the four buckets

BucketSpecific causesMechanism
↓ Renal excretion (most chronic cases)AKI & CKD; hypoaldosteronism / type-4 RTA (diabetes); Addison's; drugs — ACEi/ARB/ARNI, MRA (spironolactone, eplerenone), K-sparing diuretics, NSAIDs, trimethoprim, heparin, calcineurin inhibitorsLow GFR, low aldosterone, or blocked distal Na⁺/ENaC → impaired distal secretion
Transcellular shift (fast, dangerous)Metabolic acidosis; insulin deficiency / DKA & HHS; β-blockers; digoxin toxicity; hypertonicity/hyperglycemia; tumor lysis, rhabdomyolysis, crush, massive hemolysis; succinylcholine; hyperkalemic periodic paralysisK⁺ moves out of cells faster than the kidney can excrete it
↑ Intake / load (only matters if excretion impaired)KCl supplements, salt substitutes (KCl), high-K diet, IV potassium, stored-blood transfusionExogenous load exceeding a limited excretory reserve
Pseudohyperkalemia (spurious — exclude first)Hemolyzed sample (commonest), fist-clenching/tourniquet, marked thrombocytosis or leukocytosis, sample delay/coldK⁺ released ex vivo in the tube — the patient is not actually hyperkalemic
The renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system. Aldosterone is the master switch for distal K⁺ secretion; every RAAS inhibitor (ACEi, ARB, renin inhibitor, MRA) reduces it — therapeutically valuable but the leading drug cause of hyperkalemia.
Npatchett, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0 — source
Dietary potassium (bananas, oranges, potatoes, tomatoes, avocado, and especially KCl "low-sodium" salt substitutes) only causes hyperkalemia when excretion is already impaired — but counseling to avoid salt substitutes is one of the highest-yield outpatient moves.
abhiriksh, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0 — source
Isolated hyperkalemia + normal ECG + no plausible cause = suspect a spurious sample. Repeat as a free-flowing, non-hemolyzed specimen (and send a plasma/heparinized K⁺ if thrombocytosis or leukocytosis is present) before treating — but never delay treatment when the ECG is abnormal or the clinical picture fits. Fist-clenching alone can raise measured K⁺ by 1–2 mmol/L (NEJM 1990).
🩺 Clinic — outpatient optimization & prevention
Assess

When to suspect

🔍

Who is at risk & how it presents

Chronic hyperkalemia is a disease of impaired excretion meeting an ongoing load. In clinic, the high-yield populations are: CKD (eGFR < 45), diabetes (type-4 RTA), heart failure on RAASi + MRA, elderly patients on ACEi/ARB + a K-sparing agent or NSAID, and anyone using a KCl salt substitute. It is usually found on a routine metabolic panel, not from symptoms.

Reality checkMost outpatient hyperkalemia is asymptomatic. The danger is that symptoms are a late, unreliable warning — so the level and the ECG, not how the patient feels, drive urgency.

Presentation — symptom / sign, approximate frequency, and why

Symptom / sign~ FrequencyWhy it happens (mechanism)
Asymptomatic (incidental lab finding)>70%Chronic slow rise; myocardium and nerves partially adapt to the depolarized resting potential
Generalized muscle weakness / fatigue40–70%*Sustained membrane depolarization inactivates fast Na⁺ channels → impaired neuromuscular excitability
Palpitations / awareness of ectopy15–40%*Conduction disturbance and ventricular ectopy from altered repolarization
Paresthesias, numbness15–40%*Altered sensory-nerve membrane excitability
Nausea, vomiting, ileus15–40%*Smooth-muscle dysfunction
Peaked T waves on ECG (objective sign)common at K>6.5, but INSENSITIVEAccelerated, more complete repolarization at mildly elevated K⁺
Ascending flaccid paralysis, areflexia<15%Profound membrane inexcitability (secondary hyperkalemic paralysis) at severe levels
Bradyarrhythmia, sine wave, cardiac arrest<15% — but lethalNa⁺-channel inactivation → conduction failure → VF / PEA / asystole

*Symptom frequencies for hyperkalemia are not precisely quantified in the literature; percentages are approximate relative frequencies among symptomatic patients and are shown to convey typical prominence, not validated epidemiology. The dominant clinical reality is that most patients are asymptomatic.

Workup

What to order & when

🧪

Labs — and what each result changes

Repeat / confirm K⁺First step for any unexpected, isolated high K⁺ with a normal ECG — free-flowing, non-hemolyzed draw; send a plasma (heparinized) K⁺ if platelets or WBC are very high (excludes pseudohyperkalemia).First
BMP / CMPK⁺, HCO₃⁻, BUN/Cr (renal function & acidosis), glucose. Defines CKD stage and acid-base contribution.Initial
12-lead ECGOrder now if K⁺ ≥ 6.0, any symptom, or a rapid rise. Look for peaked T, PR prolongation, wide QRS. A normal ECG does not exclude danger.If K≥6 / symptoms
Medication reviewThe single highest-yield step: RAASi/ARNI, MRA, K-sparing diuretics, NSAIDs, trimethoprim, heparin, calcineurin inhibitors, K⁺ supplements, salt substitutes.Every visit
Venous blood gas / HCO₃⁻If metabolic acidosis is suspected (CKD, DKA) — acidosis both shifts K⁺ out and signals a treatable driver.If acidosis
Renin, aldosterone, 8 AM cortisol / cosyntropinIf hyperkalemia is unexplained or out of proportion to renal function — evaluate for hypoaldosteronism / adrenal insufficiency.If unexplained
CK, LDH, uric acid, phosphate, Ca²⁺If tissue breakdown suspected — rhabdomyolysis (CK) or tumor lysis (uric acid, phosphate, LDH, low Ca).If lysis
Digoxin levelIf on digoxin — toxicity poisons the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase and raises K⁺; a high level changes management (DigiFab).If on digoxin
How the number can lieFalsely high: hemolysis (commonest), fist-clenching/tourniquet, thrombocytosis/leukocytosis, prolonged sample transit, cold storage. Falsely reassuring (truly high but labile): a K⁺ measured before an ongoing shift (DKA being treated, continuing rhabdo/TLS) can rebound upward — recheck. Serum runs higher than plasma when platelets/WBC are elevated because K⁺ is released during clotting.
Calculator · Transtubular potassium gradient (TTKG)

A classic (now largely historical) estimate of aldosterone-driven distal K⁺ secretion. TTKG = (Urine K⁺ ÷ Plasma K⁺) ÷ (Urine osm ÷ Plasma osm). Valid only when urine osm > serum osm and urine Na⁺ > 25. In hyperkalemia a TTKG < 7–8 suggests hypoaldosteronism (the kidney should be excreting more K⁺). Assumptions about medullary osmolality have made it fall out of favor — interpret with caution.

Chronic management

💊

Stepwise therapy — first-line → escalation

The governing principle (KDIGO 2024): in CKD/HF, manage the potassium so you can keep the RAAS inhibitor, rather than stopping a drug that improves survival. Stopping RAASi for hyperkalemia is associated with higher mortality and cardiovascular events. Dose reduction/discontinuation of RAASi is the last resort, not the first. KDIGO 2024.
1
Diet + remove the offenders
Lowest-risk, highest-yield first move.
▾
Cuts the load side of the balance and restores excretion capacity by unblocking the distal nephron.
  • Dietary K⁺ restriction ~2–3 g/day (≈50–75 mmol) — dietitian referral; the biggest single win is stopping KCl "low-sodium" salt substitutes. KDOQI/KDIGO 2024
  • Stop or swap culprit drugs: NSAIDs → acetaminophen; trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole → alternative antibiotic; discontinue K⁺ supplements and K-sparing diuretics (amiloride/triamterene) when not essential.
  • For RAASi/MRA: prefer to enable (steps 2–3) rather than stop, unless K⁺ is dangerously high or refractory.
2
Add a diuretic ± sodium bicarbonate
Enhance renal K⁺ loss; correct acidosis.
▾
Loop/thiazide diuretics raise distal Na⁺ delivery and tubular flow → kaliuresis. Correcting metabolic acidosis with bicarbonate shifts K⁺ back into cells and improves renal handling.
DrugStartTitration → target / maxWhy it worksCaution / alternative
Furosemide (loop; default)20–40 mg PO dailyDouble as needed; CKD needs higher doses (up to 80–160 mg); torsemide/bumetanide if poor absorption↑ distal flow → kaliuresis; also treats volume overloadSulfa cross-reaction is rare; if true intolerance use ethacrynic acid (non-sulfonamide loop)
Torsemide / bumetanideTorsemide 10–20 mg daily · bumetanide 0.5–1 mg dailyTitrate to effect; more reliable oral bioavailability than furosemideSame loop mechanism, better/steadier absorptionBumetanide 1 mg ≈ furosemide 40 mg
Thiazide (adjunct)Hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily · chlorthalidone 12.5–25 mgAdd to a loop for synergy if eGFR > 30Distal Na⁺ blockade → kaliuresis; weak if eGFR < 30Metolazone if eGFR low and loop alone inadequate
Sodium bicarbonate650 mg PO BID–TID (or to normalize serum HCO₃⁻)Titrate to serum HCO₃⁻ 22–24; used when CKD metabolic acidosis presentCorrects acidosis → intracellular K⁺ shift + better renal excretionWatch Na⁺/volume in HF; sodium citrate alternative
3
Chronic potassium binders — to enable RAASi/MRA
Patiromer or SZC; SPS is the old, riskier resin.
▾
Binders trap K⁺ in the gut lumen for fecal excretion, lowering serum K⁺ enough to continue prognostically important RAASi/MRA (OPAL-HK, AMETHYST-DN, DIAMOND).
BinderStartTitration → target / maxWhy it worksWatch / caution
Patiromer (Veltassa)8.4 g PO once dailyTitrate at ≥1-week intervals by 8.4 g → max 25.2 g/dayCalcium-based non-absorbed polymer; exchanges Ca²⁺ for K⁺ in the colonDelayed onset (~7 h) — NOT for emergencies; hypomagnesemia, constipation; separate other oral drugs by ≥3 h or take with food. FDA label
Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (SZC, Lokelma)Chronic: 10 g PO once daily (acute correction 10 g TID up to 48 h)Titrate weekly by 5 g; usual range 5 g every-other-day → 15 g dailySelective inorganic cation exchanger; captures K⁺ throughout the GI tract; faster onset (~1 h)Edema from sodium load — caution in HF/volume overload; not for emergency use (delayed). FDA label
Sodium polystyrene sulfonate (SPS, Kayexalate)15–30 g PO (or PR)Once–several times daily; slow, unreliableOld cation-exchange resin (Na⁺ for K⁺) in the colonRisk of intestinal necrosis, esp. with sorbitol / ileus / post-op / constipation — largely superseded by patiromer & SZC. FDA warning
If the home/prior binder dose is unknown, restart at the lowest label dose (patiromer 8.4 g daily or SZC 5–10 g daily), recheck K⁺ in ~1 week, and titrate — do not assume the previous maintenance dose.
4
Refractory / specialist
Nephrology; RAASi dose change as last resort; dialysis in ESRD.
▾
  • Nephrology referral for persistent hyperkalemia despite diet + diuretic + binder, or advancing CKD.
  • Only after the above fail: reduce or stop the RAASi/MRA — documenting the trade-off against its survival benefit.
  • Maintenance dialysis in ESRD manages chronic hyperkalemia; reinforce interdialytic K⁺ restriction and salt-substitute avoidance.
Interactions

Comorbidities & drugs to avoid

🔗

How comorbidities change the course and the management

ComorbidityEffect on hyperkalemiaHow it changes management
CKD / ESRDDominant cause — reduced GFR cuts excretion; worsened by acidosis & RAASiDiet + loop diuretic + binder to preserve RAASi (KDIGO 2024); dialysis in ESRD
Heart failure (HFrEF)RAASi + MRA are prognostically essential but hyperkalemia-proneUse a binder to stay on guideline-directed therapy (DIAMOND); prefer patiromer over SZC if volume-overloaded (SZC adds sodium)
Diabetes mellitusType-4 RTA / hyporeninemic hypoaldosteronism + insulin deficiency reduce both excretion and cellular uptakeOptimize glycemic control; fludrocortisone occasionally used for isolated hypoaldosteronism; caution with RAASi + MRA stacking
Adrenal insufficiency (Addison's)Aldosterone deficiency → hyperkalemia + hyponatremiaTreat the deficiency (hydrocortisone + fludrocortisone); hyperkalemia resolves with replacement
Digoxin therapyToxicity poisons Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase → hyperkalemia (a marker of severe toxicity)Definitive therapy is digoxin-specific antibody (DigiFab); give IV calcium cautiously (see ICU)
Drugs to avoid / use with caution in a hyperkalemia-prone patient: KCl salt substitutes & K⁺ supplements · NSAIDs · trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (choose an alternative antibiotic when possible) · K-sparing diuretics (amiloride, triamterene) · avoid stacking two RAAS blockers (ACEi + ARB) · watch heparin and calcineurin inhibitors (tacrolimus, cyclosporine) · reduce and monitor MRA doses (or add a binder to continue where prognostically indicated).
Monitor

Titration & follow-up

📈

What to recheck, and when

  • After any med change, binder start, or titration: recheck serum K⁺ (and Cr) in ~1 week.
  • Starting or up-titrating a RAASi/MRA: check K⁺ and Cr at 1–2 weeks, then periodically.
  • On patiromer: also monitor magnesium (hypomagnesemia is common).
  • Once stable: K⁺ every 1–3 months, and with any intercurrent illness, dehydration, or AKI.
  • Re-counsel on salt substitutes and NSAIDs at each visit — recidivism is the usual cause of recurrence.
Prevent

Prevention & screening context

🛡️

What the evidence does — and does not — recommend

On USPSTFThere is no USPSTF Grade A or B recommendation specific to hyperkalemia (it is a laboratory consequence of other conditions, not a screening target), and the USPSTF has an I statement (insufficient evidence) on screening for CKD in asymptomatic adults. Prevention is therefore built on managing the drivers rather than a screening test.

Prevention essentials (highest yield first)

  • Medication reconciliation at every visit — the commonest reversible cause is an avoidable drug combination.
  • Baseline + follow-up K⁺/Cr when starting or up-titrating RAASi/MRA (especially in CKD, diabetes, HF, or the elderly).
  • Counsel against KCl salt substitutes and unsupervised K⁺ supplements in at-risk patients.
  • Sick-day guidance: hold RAASi/diuretics during dehydrating illness (vomiting, diarrhea, poor intake) to prevent AKI-driven hyperkalemia.
  • Treat metabolic acidosis in CKD and optimize glycemic control (reduces type-4 RTA burden).
Escalate

When to refer / admit

🚑

Red flags → ED / admission

Send to the ED / admit for any of: K⁺ ≥ 6.0–6.5 mmol/L; any ECG change (peaked T and beyond); new muscle weakness, paralysis, or palpitations; oliguria / suspected AKI; an ongoing K⁺ source (rhabdomyolysis, tumor lysis); or a patient who cannot reliably repeat labs / be monitored in the outpatient setting.
When you send a patient in, tell them to go by ambulance (not to drive) and phone ahead — a K⁺ of 7 can arrest en route, and EMS can start monitoring and treatment.
🛏️ Wards — acute inpatient management
Admit

Who to admit

📋

Admission criteria & initial profile

Admit — usually to a monitored bed / telemetry — for any of:

  • K⁺ ≥ 6.0–6.5 mmol/L (any level ≥ 6.5 warrants active treatment and monitoring).
  • Any ECG change attributable to hyperkalemia (peaked T and beyond).
  • Symptoms — weakness, paralysis, palpitations.
  • AKI / oliguria or an ongoing potassium source (rhabdomyolysis, tumor lysis, crush, GI bleed with transfusion).
  • Hyperkalemia that will not correct outpatient or a patient who cannot be reliably monitored.
Frame the case on admission by level × ECG × trajectory × cause. A stable dialysis patient at 6.4 pre-HD is different from a 6.4 climbing in crush injury — the latter needs ICU-level vigilance even at the same number.

Treat

Acute management — the cocktail

💊

Stabilize → Shift → Remove (exact doses)

If K⁺ ≥ 6.5 or any ECG change: give IV calcium first, then start shifting and removing in parallel. A shift agent without a removal plan just buys time before rebound.
1
① Stabilize the membrane — IV calcium
First if ECG changes or K⁺ ≥ 6.5. Does NOT lower K⁺.
▾
Raises the threshold potential back away from the depolarized resting potential, restoring the safety gap and protecting against arrhythmia. Onset 1–3 min, lasts 30–60 min — redose if ECG changes persist or recur.
AgentDose (US convention)Dose (UK Kidney Assoc 2023)Why / notesCaution
Calcium gluconate 10%1000 mg = 10 mL IV over 2–3 min; repeat in 5 min if ECG unchanged30 mL (6.8 mmol) over ~10 min — higher dose to avoid under-treatmentPreferred peripheral salt (less caustic); ~⅓ the elemental Ca of chlorideDo not run in the same line as sodium bicarbonate → CaCO₃ precipitates
Calcium chloride 10%500–1000 mg = 5–10 mL via central / large-bore line10 mL (6.8 mmol) — preferred in arrest / peri-arrest~3× the elemental calcium; faster in a crashing patientVesicant — tissue necrosis on extravasation; central access preferred

Sources: AHA ACLS 2020; UK Kidney Association 2023; onset/duration EMCrit IBCC.

Calcium gluconate — the first drug in the emergency: it stabilizes the myocardium within 1–3 minutes but does not lower potassium. Always follow with shift + removal.
AAAndrey A, Wikimedia Commons, Public domain — source
2
② Shift K⁺ into cells
Insulin + glucose is first-line lowering; albuterol is additive.
▾
Insulin and β2-agonists stimulate the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase to drive K⁺ into cells. Effect is temporary (~2–6 h) → K⁺ rebounds, so always pair with a removal plan.

Calculator · K⁺ severity & emergency action

Combines the serum level, the ECG, and symptoms into a band and the immediate action. Bands follow the UK Kidney Association 2023; any ECG change is treated as an emergency regardless of level.

Assessment
—
Calculator · Insulin + dextrose shift-dose helper

Standard shift dose is regular insulin 10 U IV + 25 g dextrose. Reduce to 5 U (≈0.1 U/kg) when hypoglycemia risk is high (renal failure, low weight, low baseline glucose). Whatever you give, check glucose hourly for 4–6 h — insulin-induced hypoglycemia is delayed.

Suggested regimen
—

Calculators are decision aids, not a substitute for clinical judgment or your institution's protocol. No validated numeric severity score exists for hyperkalemia — for related tools (e.g., corrected calcium, anion gap) see MDCalc.

Monitor

What to trend

📈

The rebound is the trap

  • Recheck K⁺ at ~1–2 h and ~4–6 h after treatment — shifts are temporary and K⁺ rebounds as insulin and albuterol wear off.
  • Capillary glucose hourly ×4–6 h after insulin (delayed hypoglycemia).
  • Continuous telemetry until K⁺ < 6.0 and stable; repeat ECG if it was abnormal.
  • Trend renal function, urine output, magnesium, and acid-base; reassess the source (is the rhabdo/TLS still releasing K⁺?).
  • Confirm offending drugs remain held; plan the durable removal step (binder ± dialysis) before shifts wear off.
Document a clear "next K⁺ due at [time]" order. The classic error is a reassuring 2-hour post-treatment level, no repeat, and a rebound arrest overnight.
Escalate

When to call ICU

⬆️

Floor → ICU triggers

Escalate to ICU / call nephrology for urgent dialysis when: K⁺ ≥ 6.5 refractory to initial medical therapy; ongoing ECG changes or any arrhythmia; hemodynamic instability; need for emergent dialysis (oliguric AKI / ESRD); or an ongoing massive K⁺ source (rhabdomyolysis, tumor lysis, crush) that outpaces shift therapy.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness: K⁺ < 5.5 mmol/L and stable off shift therapy (no rebound on serial levels), ECG normalized, the driver identified and addressed, offending drugs adjusted, and a concrete outpatient plan — diet counseling, a binder if chronic, held/renegotiated culprit meds, and a follow-up K⁺ within ~1 week.

Home

Stable K⁺, reversible cause fixed, reliable follow-up labs arranged.

Home health

Needs in-home lab draws / medication management (e.g., new binder, frail elderly).

SNF

Medically stable but needs skilled nursing / monitored medication administration.

Outpatient dialysis

ESRD — ensure a scheduled dialysis slot and interdialytic K⁺ plan before discharge.

Nephrology clinic

Recurrent/refractory hyperkalemia or advancing CKD → early specialist follow-up.

Hospice / palliative

If hyperkalemia reflects end-stage disease and goals are comfort-focused.
🫀 ICU — critical care & organ support
Admit

ICU triggers

🚨

When it belongs in the unit

  • K⁺ ≥ 6.5 with advanced ECG changes (wide QRS, sine wave, brady) or any arrhythmia.
  • Hemodynamic instability or peri-arrest from hyperkalemia.
  • Need for emergent hemodialysis — refractory hyperkalemia, oliguric AKI, or ESRD without residual clearance.
  • Ongoing massive potassium release — tumor lysis, rhabdomyolysis, crush — that outpaces shift therapy and will recur.
  • Post-hyperkalemic cardiac arrest.
Severe hyperkalemia with a sine wave is a peri-arrest rhythm. Give IV calcium immediately, call for dialysis, and treat empirically — do not wait for a confirmatory level.
Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, labs, targets

  • Continuous cardiac monitoring; defibrillator/pacing pads on the patient for severe cases.
  • Serial K⁺ every 1–2 h during active treatment and 1–2 h after each dialysis run (rebound).
  • Dialysis access: temporary large-bore HD catheter (IJ/femoral) if no functioning fistula/graft/tunneled line.
  • Central venous access for calcium chloride and for reliable drug delivery; arterial line if unstable or on vasoactives.
  • Hourly glucose after insulin; trend Mg, phosphate, Ca²⁺, acid-base, and the causative labs (CK, uric acid).
Remove

Emergent hemodialysis

🩺

The definitive removal — indications & the choice of modality

Indications: severe or refractory hyperkalemia — especially with oliguric AKI or ESRD, failure of/incomplete response to medical therapy, or ongoing K⁺ generation outstripping shifts. Hemodialysis removes tens of mmol of potassium within the first hour — far faster than any pharmacologic move.

ModalityWhen to chooseNotes
Intermittent hemodialysis (IHD)Default for acute severe hyperkalemia — fastest clearanceLow-K⁺ dialysate (often 1–2 mmol/L); expect rebound as intracellular K⁺ re-equilibrates — recheck K⁺ 1–2 h post-run
CRRT (CVVH/CVVHDF)Patient too hemodynamically unstable to tolerate IHDSlower clearance but continuous and gentle on hemodynamics; good for ongoing release (TLS/rhabdo)
A very low dialysate potassium clears K⁺ fastest but can provoke arrhythmia from too-rapid a drop and rebound afterward — balance speed against stability, and avoid stacking a glucose-free dialysate on top of insulin (compounding hypoglycemia).
Hemodialysis is the definitive removal step for refractory or oliguric hyperkalemia — the "emergency fire door" of the crowded-room analogy.
Виталий Поспелов, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0 — source
Arrest

Hyperkalemic arrest & airway

⛑️

ACLS modifications, circulatory support, and the RSI trap

Hyperkalemia is a reversible cause of cardiac arrest and PEA/asystole. AHA ACLS 2020 (Part 10) modifications when hyperkalemia is known or strongly suspected:

  • IV calcium chloride 1 g (10 mL of 10%) — given empirically, without waiting for a confirmatory level. (Calcium is not routine in undifferentiated arrest — hyperkalemia is a specific exception.)
  • Insulin + glucose and nebulized albuterol to shift; sodium bicarbonate 50 mEq IV if metabolic acidosis is documented.
  • Arrange emergent dialysis; prolonged resuscitation is reasonable while the reversible cause is corrected.

Source: AHA ACLS 2020, Electrolyte Abnormalities.

Peri-arrest circulatory / chronotropic support

AgentReceptors / mechanismDoseEffectWhen to pick
Epinephrineβ1, β2, α1Arrest: 1 mg IV q3–5 min · Peri-arrest infusion 0.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min↑ HR, ↑ contractility, ↑ SVRHyperkalemic bradycardia/hypotension not responding to calcium
Isoproterenolβ1, β2 (pure chronotrope)2–10 mcg/min IV↑ HRBradycardia bridge to pacing/dialysis (rarely)
Transcutaneous / transvenous pacingDirect electrical captureSet rate; capture thresholdMaintains rateSymptomatic hyperkalemic bradyarrhythmia — note capture is often difficult until K⁺ falls
NoteAtropine and pacing frequently fail in hyperkalemic bradyarrhythmia because the conduction block is metabolic, not vagal — the real fix is calcium + potassium removal (dialysis), not chronotropes.
Airway / RSI trap — avoid succinylcholine. Depolarizing paralytics raise serum K⁺ by ~0.5 mmol/L (far more in burns, crush, denervation, prolonged immobility) and can precipitate arrest in an already-hyperkalemic patient. Use rocuronium instead if intubation is required.
Rescue

Treat the ongoing source

⚙️

Because a live source keeps re-flooding the room

SourceSpecific therapyKey point
Tumor lysis syndromeAggressive IV hydration; rasburicase for hyperuricemia; cardiac monitoring; early dialysisContraindicated: rasburicase in G6PD deficiency. Avoid calcium for asymptomatic hypocalcemia (Ca-phosphate precipitation). K⁺ recurs while lysis continues.
Rhabdomyolysis / crushAggressive crystalloid to maintain urine output; treat hyperkalemia; early dialysis if oliguric/refractoryMuscle keeps releasing K⁺ (and phosphate, myoglobin) — anticipate rebound.
Digoxin toxicityDigoxin-specific antibody (DigiFab) is definitive; hyperkalemia is a marker of severe toxicityHistoric "stone heart" fear of IV calcium is largely a myth (Levine) — give slowly if needed, but the fix is DigiFab.
DKA / HHSInsulin + fluids treat the cause; total-body K⁺ is usually depletedK⁺ will fall sharply with treatment — start K⁺ replacement once K⁺ < 5.2 and urine output confirmed.
Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

Step down when K⁺ < 6.0 and falling, ECG normalized, no arrhythmia off continuous monitoring, the potassium source is controlled, no imminent dialysis need, and hemodynamics are stable off vasoactive support.
Not yet if…the K⁺ is only transiently controlled by shifts (insulin/albuterol still active), the source is still releasing (rising CK, ongoing lysis), the patient is dialysis-dependent with a pending run, or serial levels still show rebound. Keep on telemetry until the trend is convincingly down without shift agents on board.
Pearls

Practice-changing pearls

💡

The fifteen things that change what you do

  1. Get an ECG in every hyperkalemia — but never rule out danger on a normal one. The ECG is insensitive; sudden hyperkalemic arrest happens with a bland tracing. Treat the level, the trajectory, and any change.
  2. Treat the number AND the patient. An emergency is defined by ECG changes, symptoms, or rate of rise — not the absolute K⁺ alone. A fast-rising 6.2 can be worse than a stable 6.8.
  3. Calcium first — but calcium doesn't lower potassium. It stabilizes the membrane for 30–60 minutes. You must follow with shift and removal or the arrhythmia risk returns.
  4. Shift is temporary → recheck K⁺ at 1–2 h and 4–6 h. Insulin and albuterol wear off and K⁺ rebounds. Never give a shift agent without a removal plan.
  5. Insulin causes delayed hypoglycemia — monitor glucose hourly for 4–6 h. Use 5 units (or 0.1 U/kg) in renal failure or low body weight, and add follow-on 10% dextrose if baseline glucose < 126 mg/dL (7 mmol/L).
  6. Don't run calcium and sodium bicarbonate through the same line — calcium carbonate precipitates. Flush between, or use separate access.
  7. Bicarbonate is not reliable K⁺-lowering monotherapy. Reserve it for metabolic acidosis; a systematic review found minimal K⁺ effect on its own.
  8. SPS (Kayexalate) can cause fatal bowel necrosis — avoid it in ileus, post-op, constipation, or uremic bowel, and never co-administer sorbitol. Prefer patiromer or SZC.
  9. Isolated hyperkalemia + normal ECG + no cause = suspect pseudohyperkalemia. Repeat a non-hemolyzed, free-flowing sample (send a plasma K⁺ if platelets/WBC are high) before treating.
  10. Binders enable RAASi/MRA — don't reflexively stop them in CKD/HF. Stopping RAASi worsens outcomes; DIAMOND showed patiromer kept ~85% of HFrEF patients on target therapy.
  11. Albuterol is blunted ~50% in ESRD and up to a third of patients are non-responders — never rely on it alone.
  12. Dialysis is the definitive fire exit. For refractory or oliguric hyperkalemia, IHD clears K⁺ faster than CRRT; expect a post-HD rebound and recheck K⁺ 1–2 h later.
  13. Calcium chloride via central/large line only (3× the elemental calcium, caustic); calcium gluconate is the safer peripheral default.
  14. In digoxin toxicity, IV calcium is likely safe (the "stone heart" is largely a myth) but give it slowly — the real fix is DigiFab.
  15. An ongoing source keeps re-flooding the room. Tumor lysis, rhabdomyolysis, and crush injury keep releasing K⁺ — anticipate recurrence and dialyze early. And avoid succinylcholine for intubation — it raises K⁺.

  • ESC 2021 Heart Failure Guideline — MRA potassium thresholds: do not start if K⁺ > 5.0; halve dose if K⁺ > 5.5; stop if K⁺ > 6.0. Eur Heart J 2021
  • Recommendations for managing hyperkalemia on RAASi (2024). PMC10954964

Landmark trials

TrialYearResultWhy it matters
PEARL-HF2011Patiromer (RLY5016) lowered K⁺ and allowed more patients to reach target spironolactone in HFFirst proof that a binder can enable MRA use
HARMONIZE (ZS-9/SZC)2014Open-label SZC 10 g TID ×48 h → normokalemia; 5/10/15 g maintenance all beat placebo over 28 d; edema dose-dependent (14% at 15 g)Basis for the SZC dosing range
OPAL-HK2015Patiromer in CKD on RAASi: ~76% normokalemic by week 4; randomized withdrawal → K⁺ rose back on placeboEstablished binder-enabled RAASi continuation (NEJM)
ZS-0032015SZC dose-dependently lowered K⁺ within 48 h vs placeboConfirmed rapid, dose-related SZC efficacy (NEJM)
AMETHYST-DN2015Patiromer in diabetic CKD: significant K⁺ fall by week 4, durable to 52 weeksLong-term efficacy/safety of chronic binding (JAMA)
ENERGIZE2021SZC added to insulin-glucose in acute ED hyperkalemia showed a trend to greater/earlier K⁺ lowering (not definitive)Explores SZC's role in the acute setting
